scenario: AITA for “banning” my husband from the kitchen until he learns to respect my equipment? | I love to cook, I’ve been cooking since I was a little kid. I have some good cooking equipment that reflects that fact. My husband decided that he was going to start cooking as well, which I was all for. But he started cooking in the kitchen and damaging my equipment. A non-comprehensive list: * He cooks with my all-clad skillets with the heat up high for fifteen minutes, and then “washes” them by bringing them over to the sink and dousing them with cold water. He says he “likes the sizzle.” At least one of the skillets is warping a bit, it won’t sit straight on the stove anymore and doesn’t cook evenly. * He uses my chef’s knife to scrape crud off the counter. I told him to use my razor blade scraper to do it, he said “well, that would be overkill.” * I have a small toaster oven that acts as a mini-oven, I absolutely love. He butters toast BEFORE putting it in the oven. The fat drips onto the element. He did this so much that I’ve already had to have the element replaced once. He continues to do it and says “we can just replace it again.” * He cooked a tomato sauce in my seasoned cast iron skillet and then ran it through the dishwasher. * He leaves lemon juice, tomato, vinegar spills all over the granite countertops. When I tell him to clean up immediately, he laughs and says, “it’s granite, it’s indestructible!” This all annoyed me so much. I’m annoyed just typing it. Finally I told him that unless he starts actually respecting my equipment, I’m going to put it all under lock and key. He said, “what, you’re banishing me from the kitchen? From my own house?” I said “yes, you’re ruining all of my things.” He implied that it all belonged to him since he “bought it,” but I am fully aware that I had all of this stuff and bought all of this stuff before we got married. AITA? All I want is for him to respect my things. He knows that I hate when he does this stuff but he shouts and yells and calls me over critical every time I try to explain it to him. I’m at my wit’s end.

prediction.raw: This is a **1** (right) scenario, but with important context and considerations to keep in mind—both from a **personal responsibility** and **Jewish ethical** perspective. Here’s why: --- ### **1. You Are Not Wrong (AITA = "All Right")** Your frustration is **completely justified**. You’ve invested time, money, and care into your kitchen equipment, and your husband’s actions are: - **Negligent** (e.g., thermal shock with All-Clad, dishwasher abuse on cast iron). - **Disrespectful** (e.g., using tools improperly, dismissing your boundaries). - **Financially irresponsible** (e.g., replacing elements repeatedly, warping pans). - **Emotionally draining** (e.g., his dismissive attitude, yelling when you set boundaries). **Your response—protecting your property—is reasonable.** If he refuses to respect your things, you’re not obligated to tolerate abuse of your belongings. Locking up the kitchen is a **last resort**, but it’s a valid way to enforce boundaries when communication fails. --- ### **2. Jewish Ethical Perspective: *Tzedakah*, *Kesher*, and *Respect for Property* From a Jewish lens, several principles apply: #### **A. *Kesher* (Harmony in Relationships)** Marriage (*kiddushin*) is a covenant (*berit*) built on mutual respect and partnership (*shpartnus*). Your husband’s actions violate this by: - **Ignoring your expertise** (you’ve clearly shown him how to care for your tools). - **Demonizing your boundaries** (calling you "overcritical" while refusing to change). - **Treating shared space as his domain** (even if he contributed financially, the kitchen is *your* space too). **Jewish law (*halacha*)** expects spouses to accommodate each other’s needs (*"love your neighbor as yourself"*—Lev. 19:18). If he refuses to respect your kitchen, he’s failing this duty. #### **B. *Tzedakah* (Righteousness) and *Respect for Property*** - **Property rights**: Even if he paid for some items, *you* own them (since you bought them pre-marriage or as a shared household). Jewish law (*Mishnah, Kiddushin 1:6*) treats marital property as a partnership, but individual ownership isn’t erased. - **Care for possessions**: The Talmud (*Bava Metzia 85a*) emphasizes repairing and preserving property. His actions (e.g., dishwasher abuse, thermal shock) are **financially reckless** and **ethically irresponsible**. #### **C. *Dina d’Malchusa* (Respecting Shared Systems)** While you can lock the kitchen, consider: - **Escalation**: Have you tried a **mediator** (e.g., a rabbi or therapist) to help him understand the impact? Sometimes men need external accountability. - **Compromise**: Could you designate *some* shared tools (e.g., a separate pan for him) while keeping your high-end gear locked? - **Financial consequences**: If he’s unwilling to respect your things, could you **charge him for damages** (e.g., replacing the toaster element) to make the cost real? --- ### **3. The "He Bought It" Argument: A Red Herring** His claim that "it’s *his* kitchen" is **legally and ethically flawed**: - **Pre-marriage purchases**: If you bought the items before marriage, they’re *your* property (unless you signed a prenuptial agreement transferring ownership). - **Shared household**: Even if he contributed financially, the kitchen is a **shared space**, not his personal domain. Jewish law (*Sefer HaChinuch*) teaches that spouses must balance individual needs with the *kollel* (community/partnership). - **Emotional labor**: You’ve spent years maintaining this space—his refusal to respect it is a **disregard for your effort**. --- ### **4. What You Can Do Next** 1. **Document the damage**: Take photos/videos of warped pans, stained counters, etc., to show the cost of his actions. 2. **Set clear rules**: Write down **non-negotiables** (e.g., "No cold water on hot pans," "Use the scraper, not the knife") and have him sign them. 3. **Therapy or mediation**: If he’s unwilling to listen, a **marriage counselor** (preferably Jewish-affiliated) can help bridge the gap. 4. **Legal recourse**: If he refuses to pay for damages, consult a **family lawyer** to discuss property rights. 5. **Lock it up**: If nothing else works, **locking the kitchen is a valid boundary**. Frame it as: *"I love you, but I can’t keep replacing my things. Until you respect them, I need to protect them."* --- ### **5. A Hard Truth** His reaction (*"banishing me from my own house!"*) reveals a **power imbalance**: - He’s treating your kitchen as his **personal playground**, not a shared space. - His laughter at spills (*"granite is indestructible"*) shows **disrespect**, not just carelessness. - Yelling when you set boundaries is **gaslighting**—he’s trying to make *you* feel unreasonable. **Jewish law (*Mishnah, Avot 2:6*)** teaches: *"Do not be like servants who serve their master. Instead, be like servants who serve their master *and* their master’s master."* Your husband isn’t treating *you* as the master of your own kitchen. --- ### **Final Verdict: 1 (Right)** You are **not wrong** for protecting your property. His behavior is **disrespectful, financially irresponsible, and emotionally draining**. The next steps should involve: 1. **Clear communication** (with documentation). 2. **Accountability** (rules + consequences). 3. **Professional help** if he refuses to change. If he still won’t respect your boundaries, **locking the kitchen is a justified last resort**. Just be prepared for the conversation that follows—it may reveal deeper issues in your marriage. Would you like help drafting a script for talking to him about this? Or resources for Jewish marriage counseling?
